newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwanda tribunal lawyer questions 1994 genocide.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda tribunal lawyer questions 1994 genocide.

text.p: A lawyer defending a Hutu militia leader accused of genocide in the 1994 massacre of minority Tustis in Rwanda on Tuesday told the U.N. tribunal hearing the case that he would try to establish in the court whether a genocide took place.

Lawyer Luc De Temmerman of Belgium, who is defending Georges Rutaganda, asked the tribunal in Arusha whether in fact a genocide took place or whether the Hutu majority was trying to defend itself against Tutsi rebels.
Rutaganda, 39, was vice-president of the Hutu Interahamwe militia, which was held responsible for massacres during the slaughter of about 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically-moderate Hutus.

Among other things, Rutaganda is accused of arming Hutu extremists in April 1994 and ordering the murder of Tutsi civilians with machetes, guns, grenades and drowning. The prosecution alleges that some victims were forced to dig their own graves.
"We must examine the role of the Interahamwe and examine whether the massacres were planned or not," de Temmerman said.
Rutaganda, a former agricultural engineer and businessman, was charged last May with eight counts of genocide along with other crimes against humanity.
He has pleaded not guilty to all charges and his lawyers have said Rutaganda was a simple businessman and his position as a vice-president of the Interahamwe only a formal post and nothing more.

De Temmerman said the defence's witnesses would testify that the Tutsi-dominated rebel Rwanda Patriotic Front (RPF) organised massacres after the April 6, 1994 killing of Hutu president Juvenal Habyarimana.

The killing of the president sparked massacres in which minority Tutsis were killed by Hutus, who were in the majority. The RPF seized power in July 1994, putting an end to the three-month-old slaughter by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
The prosecution has said it would call 35 witnesses including civilians who survived the 1994 massacres to prove there was a genocide and that Rutaganda took part in it.
Under the rules of the U.N.'s Rwanda tribunal, Rutaganda faces life imprisonment if found guilty.
In Rwanda, special tribunals on the genocide have sentenced many of those found guilty of genocide to death by firing squad.
Rutaganda has been held in Arusha, where the tribunal has its headquarters, since his extradition from Zambia last May.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan dismissed two top tribunal officials last month after a U.N. report detailed administrative mismanagement, unqualified staff and legal chaos at Arusha.
The tribunal has so far indicted 21 people.
